This study examines the dynamic and thermodynamic characteristics of a model polymer system across a broad spectrum of temperatures and molecular weights. We analyze the temperature-dependent behavior of the structural relaxation time, glass transition temperature ($T_g$), Kauzmann temperature ($T_K$), and configurational entropy ($S_c$) as functions of molecular weight. Furthermore, we explore the correlations between $T_K$ and $S_c$ alongside $T_g$ and $T_K$ to evaluate the thermodynamic-dynamic link. Our findings indicate that the ratio $T_K/T_g$ remains constant regardless of molecular weight, suggesting that the thermodynamic-dynamic relationship is independent of chain length.

Transformer-based language models have achieved remarkable success across numerous natural language processing tasks. However, their training and inference processes are computationally expensive, prompting researchers to explore methods for reducing model size and complexity. This study investigates the phenomenon of "denial processing" in transformer language models, where the model learns to disregard specific tokens during generation. We demonstrate that this behavior can be leveraged to decrease inference costs by masking the generation of tokens that the model effectively denies. Our findings indicate that this masking strategy maintains generation quality while offering significant computational savings.

Neural machine translation (NMT) models typically rely on an attention mechanism to simulate translation memory, yet this standard approach is constrained by its inability to access future tokens in the target sentence. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a forward-looking attention mechanism designed to enhance production-based NMT models. Empirical results demonstrate that this method improves BLEU scores across multiple languages and datasets, with the most significant gains observed in low-resource scenarios.

We calculate the Kontsevich weights for curvature and link graphs within symplectic Poisson manifolds, demonstrating that these values are rational numbers. This result stems from the observation that the relevant graph sums correspond to specific residues of integrals defined over the moduli space of punctured Riemann spheres. By employing the Drinfeld associator, we explicitly evaluate these curvature graph contributions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these computed graph weights and those of the MUM (Manin-Mumford) modular graphs.

We establish a large-$N$ framework for analyzing arbitrary interactions within large-$N$ conformal field theories (CFTs), utilizing the holographic duality between CFTs and gravity theories on asymptotically anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetimes. By examining the bulk dynamics, we demonstrate that the thermal entropy of such interacting CFTs, when scaled by $N^2$, remains identical to that of the free CFT. This finding contrasts with the behavior of entanglement entropy, which exhibits significant variations across different interactions. We further explore the implications of these results for the black hole information paradox.
This paper presents a concise proof of the comprehensive framework for pricing Asian options under Markov processes, as originally proposed by Linetsky (2002).

Clusters of galaxies are recognized as the most luminous sources of X-rays and radio waves in the universe. This study investigates their gamma-ray emission, which has been detected from several clusters by the Fermi-LAT telescope. We present a comprehensive analysis of the gamma-ray fluxes from 10 Fermi-LAT-detected clusters, alongside flux estimates for 10 additional clusters not seen by Fermi-LAT. Our results indicate that the average gamma-ray flux per cluster is approximately $10^{-12}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$, a value that is roughly 100 times greater than the average flux from the entire sky. This suggests that the gamma-ray background observed by Fermi-LAT is dominated by emission from galaxy clusters.

We investigate the primordial signatures of heavy primordial fluctuations in the early universe, specifically examining how they imprint on the primordial power spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the distinctive "cosmological collider" signatures—namely oscillatory patterns and specific non-Gaussianity—are contingent upon the initial state of these fluctuations. We demonstrate that when primordial fluctuations originate from the ground state, the oscillatory features in the power spectrum are suppressed. Consequently, the traditional cosmological collider signals, which rely on these oscillations, are absent in this scenario. Furthermore, we explore the implications of the "primal feature" hypothesis, which posits that primordial fluctuations begin in the ground state. Our findings indicate that while the primal feature hypothesis eliminates the conventional cosmological collider signals, it simultaneously offers a viable pathway to detect primordial heavy particles through alternative non-Gaussianity signatures.

Although deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in computer vision, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This study introduces a novel framework designed to interpret CNNs by linking their hidden layers to semantic concepts. The proposed method employs a specialized filter attention mechanism to establish these connections, enabling the visualization of how specific concepts are represented within the network's internal filters. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the generation of novel concepts by optimizing filter weights to maximize the alignment between learned representations and target concept data. The effectiveness of this framework is validated through two key applications: visualizing the semantic content of filter representations and performing zero-shot classification.

This study investigates the role of phonons in mediating attractive interactions between electrons in one-dimensional cuprates, a class of materials renowned for their high-temperature superconductivity. We demonstrate that phonon-mediated coupling can generate long-range interactions, a finding that contrasts with the short-range nature of the conventional electron-phonon interaction. Furthermore, we show that these interactions can induce superconductivity in one-dimensional cuprates, a phenomenon that aligns with experimental observations of the pseudogap phase.

This study examines the causal relationships within the MPHIA individual dataset, which comprises 1,000 participants from the 2016 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). The analysis utilizes the Ising model to represent the system's structure, with the Ising Hamiltonian's parameters estimated via the pseudo-likelihood method. The resulting causal graph reveals that the system is dominated by a single, highly influential node, which exerts significant influence on the majority of other variables.

The emergence of magnetic skyrmions in chiral magnets has garnered significant attention due to their potential applications in spintronics. While the skyrmion lattice (SkL) in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ is known to be metastable, its stability is compromised by geometric melting at elevated temperatures. This study investigates the SkL melting process in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ by analyzing the temperature-dependent evolution of the magnetic structure, as revealed through neutron diffraction. The findings indicate that the SkL undergoes a transition from a hexagonal to a square lattice at approximately 100 K, a phenomenon attributed to the thermal expansion of the unit cell. Furthermore, the temperature at which the SkL vanishes is observed to be lower than the temperature at which the square lattice forms.

Dynamic influence models are employed to examine how individuals' behaviors are shaped by their social networks, a process that unfolds over time. While foundational studies typically focused on low-dimensional scenarios involving a limited number of actors, recent advancements have introduced high-dimensional extensions capable of handling large-scale networks. This review offers a selective overview of current high-dimensional dynamic influence model methodologies and outlines potential future research directions.

This study investigates the stable point approach to solving balance problems, initially establishing the existence of such stable points within convex sets under specific conditions. Furthermore, we present an iterative algorithm designed to approximate these stable points, demonstrating its convergence under suitable assumptions. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our findings by addressing several balance-related challenges, including the generalized split common fixed point problem, the minimization of a convex function, the computation of common fixed points for a family of nonexpansive mappings, and the determination of common fixed points for two strongly pseudocontractive mappings.

This study introduces a novel approach to applying Bayesian neural networks in the realm of reversible data concealment. We demonstrate that Bayesian networks can learn effective mappings for data expansion and compression, enabling the embedding of additional information within host images. This method offers a significant advantage by eliminating the need for training data, thereby enhancing the flexibility of the concealment process. We evaluate our technique against established methods, specifically the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and the U-Net architectures, using both synthetic and real-world images. The experimental results indicate that our Bayesian network model achieves superior performance in terms of Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) compared to these existing approaches.

The mean-field framework is a standard method for investigating the generation of global dynamo action, yet it relies on several simplifying assumptions. Specifically, it models the impact of small-scale turbulence on large-scale magnetic fields using only two parameters: the turbulent magnetic diffusivity and the turbulent magnetic pumping effect. This study examines the limitations of such assumptions by analyzing the dynamo spectrum of a spherical shell subjected to uniform rotation and a uniform magnetic field. The findings indicate that the mean-field framework fails to accurately capture the dynamo spectrum in this scenario. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the dynamo spectrum is highly sensitive to the influence of small-scale turbulence, which cannot be adequately represented by the traditional two-parameter approach.

Outflows are a common feature of starburst galaxies, yet their origins and impacts remain uncertain. This study presents the first ALMA observations of a molecular outflow in NGC4945, a nearby starburst galaxy. The data reveal a CO(2-1) outflow extending 1.5 kpc from the galaxy's center with a velocity width of 100 km/s. The outflow's morphology is highly elongated, with an axis ratio of 1:3, and is oriented nearly perpendicular to the galaxy's disk. The outflow's kinematics are consistent with a bipolar structure, and its spatial distribution aligns with the galaxy's magnetic field. The outflow's mass is estimated at 1.5 x 10^7 solar masses, with a mass outflow rate of 1.5 x 10^2 solar masses per year. Quasilinear diffusion theory is a fundamental tool for modeling transport in magnetized plasmas, yet it poses significant numerical challenges due to its hyperbolic nature, which can lead to non-physical solutions. This study introduces a Galerkin solver for the associated hyperbolic framework that conserves both energy and the quasilinear momentum. By employing a conservative finite element approach, the method ensures the preservation of these physical invariants. Furthermore, a novel technique is developed to calculate the quasilinear momentum directly from the hyperbolic solution, eliminating the need for post-processing. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this solver is robust and efficient, successfully resolving the complexities of quasilinear diffusion.

This study introduces Variable Stepsize Semi-Discontinuous Implicit Midpoint methods (VSS-SDIMSIM) for solving standard ordinary and first-order differential equations. These methods are derived by applying the SDIMSIM framework to the standard equation formulation. The SDIMSIM method, a member of the class of semi-discontinuous Runge-Kutta methods, is noted for its high order of accuracy, algebraic stability, and conservation properties. Furthermore, the SDIMSIM class supports the development of variable stepsize solvers. This paper establishes the existence and uniqueness of the solution for the SDIMSIM method, analyzes its order of accuracy and stability, and demonstrates its ability to conserve energy in Hamiltonian systems. Additionally, the study addresses the construction of variable stepsize SDIMSIM methods, proves their solvability, and evaluates their order and stability characteristics.

This study establishes a condition for the exponential stability of a $C_0$-semigroup on a Banach space, building upon the findings in reference [1]. The proposed criterion is expressed in terms of the existence of a specific operator $P$ that satisfies a particular Lyapunov equation.

This study introduces MuMuPy, an open-source Python package designed to compute the differential cross section for muonium and dimuonium scattering off matter. The underlying framework relies on the non-relativistic Born approximation, utilizing the Upsilon potential for dimuonium and the Schrödinger equation for muonium. The package offers precomputed wave functions for the ground states of both systems, alongside analytical expressions for the static electric and electric dipole polarizabilities of dimuonium. Furthermore, MuMuPy calculates the differential cross section for the interaction of dimuonium with a hydrogen atom in its ground state, as well as with a hydrogen-like ion.

This study investigates the optimal portfolio selection problem for a power utility function that depends on both total and relative wealth. The analysis is conducted within a complete market framework featuring a risk-free asset and $d$ risky assets, where the dynamics of the risky assets are modeled as a multi-dimensional geometric Brownian motion. The resulting optimal wealth dynamics are derived as a solution to a system of coupled stochastic differential equations. Furthermore, the study establishes the asymptotic behavior of the optimal wealth process as the investment horizon extends indefinitely.

This study reviews the IGM of dwarf galaxies, focusing on the physical and chemical characteristics of their circumgalactic medium (CGM) and the intergalactic medium (IGM) beyond the virial radius. We investigate the breakdown of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermionic system coupled to local bosons, focusing on the interplay between the quasiparticle lifetime and the bosonic correlation length. Our analysis reveals that quasiparticles can fail in an unconventional manner: even when the quasiparticle lifetime remains short, they may still be well-defined provided the bosonic correlation length is sufficiently short. This finding is illustrated by examining the interaction between electrons and spin fluctuations within a ferromagnet. In this context, we demonstrate that the standard description of the electron self-energy, which relies on the quasiparticle approximation, becomes invalid. Furthermore, we show that the non-Fermi-liquid behavior observed in such systems is not merely a consequence of the quasiparticle failure itself, but rather a distinct physical phenomenon.

This study examines the divergent properties of braided-Thompson groups and the generalized Thompson groups $F_n$ and $V_n$. We demonstrate that the divergence of $F_n$ and $V_n$ is of linear type, whereas braided-Thompson groups exhibit constant divergence. Additionally, we establish that the divergence of $F_n$ and $V_n$ is governed by the constant function $d_2$.

This study presents a comprehensive end-to-end Question-Answering framework utilizing the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approach. We evaluate the performance of the system when trained on the Natural Questions dataset, employing a pre-trained Dense Passage Retriever (DPR) for the retrieval stage and a pre-trained T5 model for the generation phase.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of orthogonal polynomials associated with the logarithmic weight function $w(x) = |x-a|^{-1}$ on the interval $[-1, 1]$, where $a$ is a fixed point within that range. Our findings indicate that the asymptotic behavior of these polynomials is governed by the location of $a$ relative to the origin. Specifically, when $a=0$, the resulting orthogonal polynomials correspond to the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind.

The Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) platform has become a primary source for crowdsourcing high-quality data, particularly for training large language models (LLMs) on tasks like summarization. However, the rapid expansion of model capabilities has created a growing demand for workers with specific expertise, raising critical questions about the availability and cost of such "expert" workers on the platform. This study investigates the feasibility of sourcing qualified experts for summarization tasks by analyzing historical MTurk data, conducting controlled experiments, and performing a cost-benefit analysis. Our findings indicate that while workers with specific summarization experience are scarce, the majority of available "experts" lack verifiable domain knowledge. Consequently, the study concludes that relying on these individuals offers no significant performance advantage over standard crowdworkers, suggesting that the costs associated with hiring them outweigh the minimal, if any, gains in output quality.

Text-video retrieval (TVR) involves aligning textual and visual data to retrieve relevant video clips based on a given query. Although current state-of-the-art methods typically rely on Transformer architectures, they often suffer from high computational costs and suboptimal performance. To address these limitations, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel framework designed to enhance both efficiency and effectiveness. TS2-Net employs a dual-stage architecture: initially, a Token Shift module dynamically adjusts the number of tokens to balance computational load and semantic representation, followed by a Choice Transformer that selectively aggregates the most pertinent features. This approach significantly boosts performance while maintaining computational efficiency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TS2-Net achieves superior results compared to existing methods, delivering a 1.5-fold reduction in FLOPs and a 1.2-fold decrease in memory usage.

We introduce a model featuring a novel $Z_2$ symmetry, which permits flavour-violating neutral currents involving the top quark. This framework allows for significant enhancements in the production of single top quarks alongside a charged scalar, as well as top-antitop pairs accompanied by a $Z$ boson. These distinctive signatures offer promising avenues for detection at the Large Hadron Collider.

This study examines a directed hybrid random network model that integrates preferential attachment (PA) and uniform attachment (UA) mechanisms. We derive the asymptotic degree distribution for both in-degrees and out-degrees, demonstrating that the resulting distributions follow a power law with an exponent dependent on the relative proportions of UA and PA. Furthermore, we analyze the average path length and establish that it scales logarithmically with the network size.

This paper introduces a wireless disturbance detection system utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) capable of identifying and classifying disturbances across multiple categories. The system leverages a multi-label CNN architecture trained on a dataset of 1,000 samples, where each sample is tagged with one or more disturbance categories. The study evaluates the system's performance against a baseline single-label CNN and a Random Forest classifier. Results indicate that the proposed multi-label CNN outperforms both comparison methods in detection accuracy and classification precision.

This study examines the dynamics of a charged Klein-Gordon particle within the Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime, representing a cylindrically symmetric solution to Einstein's field equations for a cosmic string. The analysis incorporates a space-like displacement vector and derives the corresponding energy spectrum alongside the associated wave functions. Furthermore, the paper investigates the correlations between energy and both charge and vorticity.

We define locally normal measure algebras as a broad category that encompasses both the measure algebras of classical Banach spaces and those of operator spaces. Our work establishes a representation theorem for these structures, demonstrating that they are isomorphic to specific locally normal subalgebras of standard measure algebras. Furthermore, we explore the structural properties of these algebras, including their Grothendieck nature, the behavior of their dual spaces, and their Grothendieck spectrum.

The alignment of the recoil proton in Deep Virtual Compton Scattering (DVCS) offers a novel means to distinguish between the two processes, DVCS and Bethe-Heitler (BH). This recoil proton alignment is defined as the angle between the recoil proton's transverse momentum and the plane containing the virtual photon and the target proton. This study examines the recoil proton alignment in the context of $e^-$-$p$ collisions at the EIC, analyzing how its dependence on the azimuthal angle of the outgoing photon can differentiate DVCS from the BH process. The analysis reveals that the alignment angle exhibits a strong sensitivity to the skewness parameter $\lambda$, which characterizes the virtual photon's transverse momentum. Consequently, the azimuthal distribution of the recoil photon in the plane of the incoming and outgoing virtual photons serves as a robust indicator for separating DVCS from BH contributions.

This paper introduces a conceptual framework for Enhanced Artificial Intelligence (EAI), a new paradigm designed to address the limitations of current Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. EAI is defined by three core pillars: (1) the integration of human intelligence with AI to create a collaborative system, (2) the application of advanced AI techniques to improve human capabilities, and (3) the implementation of ethical guidelines to ensure responsible AI deployment. The proposed model offers a pathway to overcome existing AI challenges, including ethical concerns, transparency issues, and the risk of job displacement.

We investigate the thermal evolution of the modulated superfluid phase within spin-orbit-coupled bosons confined to a three-dimensional optical lattice. By employing a self-consistent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov framework, we determine the thermal displacement of the superfluid phase as a function of temperature and chemical potential. Our analysis reveals that the shift exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on temperature, featuring a distinct peak at an intermediate thermal regime. Furthermore, we examine the influence of varying spin-orbit coupling strengths and optical lattice depths on this thermal displacement.

We demonstrate that the automorphism group of a graph with an Abelian group $G$ as its realization group exhibits a specific structural property: it is a $p$-group for any prime $p$ dividing the order of $G$. This finding confirms a conjecture proposed by the second and third authors in 2016. Additionally, we establish that the diameter of such graphs is bounded by $O(\log |G|)$, thereby extending a result by Godsil and Hahn from 1993. We also provide a counterexample to a conjecture by the second author from 2016, which concerned the relationship between the graph's automorphism group and its Abelian realization group.

We investigate holographic duality between type IIA string theory on $AdS_3 \times S^2 \times T^3$ and three-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=4$ supersymmetric $U(1)^3$ Chern-Simons-matter theory. By examining the supersymmetric index, we identify a new supersymmetric phase and derive the corresponding Bekenstein-Hawking entropy for the associated supersymmetric micro black holes. Additionally, we calculate the supersymmetric index for the dual field theory, which aligns perfectly with the holographic predictions.

Gaussian process (GP) kernels serve as the cornerstone for defining the characteristics of latent functions within GP regression and classification. While numerous kernel designs exist, many are derived from physical principles or empirical observations rather than fundamental mathematical constructs. This paper introduces a systematic method for constructing kernels directly from basic mathematical expressions. By leveraging this approach, we demonstrate the creation of novel kernels that accurately model functions exhibiting specific behaviors, such as periodicity, symmetry, and polynomial trends.

The muon collider is a proposed accelerator facility that offers significant potential for probing physics beyond the Standard Model. However, muon beams generate intense synchrotron radiation, which can cause detrimental effects such as beam loss, emittance growth, and equipment damage. This paper examines various strategies for mitigating this noise, including shielding, noise filtering, and noise reduction through beam manipulation. We analyze the trade-offs between these approaches and propose a roadmap for future research to address the challenges posed by muon-induced noise.

Sparsity is a highly sought-after trait in deep learning, offering benefits such as reduced memory usage, faster inference, and diminished training costs. However, current sparse neural network (SNN) approaches face significant hurdles: they rely on heuristic quantization and binarization, necessitate specialized hardware, and often suffer from degraded performance. This paper introduces Spartan, a novel framework that enables sparse deep learning without these limitations. Spartan utilizes a differentiable, regularized optimization approach to train SNNs, ensuring that the resulting sparse weights are exactly representable in floating-point format. By employing a regularized optimization objective, Spartan achieves superior accuracy compared to existing SNN methods. Furthermore, Spartan offers flexible control over sparsity levels and supports various sparsity patterns, including structured and unstructured configurations.

This study investigates the emergence of an effective Pauli exclusion principle within a bosonic fluid, driven by the coupling between bosons and fermionic quasiparticles. We demonstrate that, in a weakly interacting boson gas, the coupling to fermionic excitations results in a substantial modification of the bosonic equation of state. This alteration is significant enough to suppress the onset of Bose-Einstein condensation at low densities. Furthermore, we show that the bosonic system's thermodynamic properties closely mirror those of a strongly repulsive fermionic gas.

Test smells, which represent common issues in test code, can detrimentally impact the efficacy of testing. Although various studies have proposed techniques to identify and eliminate these odors, there remains a lack of empirical data regarding their severity from a developer's perspective. This study addresses that gap by surveying 100 developers to assess how critical test smells are. The findings reveal that developers generally view test odors as a significant concern, with the majority indicating a strong desire to address them.

This study investigates a non-convex integral-differential inclusion defined by a set-valued map that is discontinuous and potentially unbounded. The analysis relies on a novel non-convex integral-differential sweeping process concept, which is established through the application of the non-convex differential inclusion theory developed by Ac\'{e}l\'{e} and Valadier. The existence of solutions to this sweeping process is proven using the Lyapunov function method combined with the theory of differential inclusions. Furthermore, the work demonstrates the applicability of this framework to optimal control problems involving systems with both delays and aftereffects.

This paper introduces KKMCee, a Monte Carlo event generator designed to simulate electron-positron annihilation into lepton or quark pairs, including the formation of resonant vector bosons. The program calculates the full matrix elements for single and double photon emission, as well as the corresponding electron and positron wave functions, incorporating the complete one-loop QED vertex correction. It also accounts for the interference between the photon and Z-boson propagators, alongside the vector and axial-vector couplings of the produced fermions. The implementation features a multi-photon Monte Carlo algorithm that models soft and collinear photon radiation, with an option to include the effects of initial-state radiation (ISR) photon polarization. The program's accuracy has been validated against analytical predictions for the total cross-section and the photon spectrum in the KKMCee process.

This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture, Tiramisu, designed to estimate inter-beat intervals (IBI) from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. The proposed method achieves superior accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques, delivering a mean IBI estimation error of 1.02 ms.

Graph embedding involves representing nodes as vectors in a low-dimensional space to preserve structural and semantic relationships. While most existing methods focus on static graphs, recent advancements have extended this to dynamic contexts by modeling graphs as sequences of snapshots over time. This paper reviews current approaches for embedding evolving graphs, categorizing them into three primary strategies: snapshot-based, temporal-aware, and time-aware methods. We analyze the strengths and limitations of each category and outline potential future research directions.

The $^7$H nucleus, a candidate for the heaviest halo nucleus, is examined using a cluster model that treats it as a $^3$H+4n excitation. This approach employs a newly developed, density-dependent, finite-range Gogny-type effective interaction to describe the four-neutron component. By utilizing a complex optical potential, the model successfully reproduces experimental elastic scattering data for $^3$H+4n collisions, yielding a binding energy of $B(^7$H$)$ = 0.85 MeV. This value aligns with recent findings from the $^3$H($^4$He,p$)$ reaction study. Furthermore, the calculated root-mean-square radii for $^7$H and its constituent $^3$H+4n system are found to be 5.1 fm and 5.2 fm, respectively, both of which are consistent with the observed halo radius of $^7$H.

This study examines the Nirenberg problem on the hemisphere $S^{n+1}/\partial S^n$ for dimensions $n \geq 3$. We establish the existence of non-conformally flat round spheres that embed isometrically into the standard sphere $S^{n+1}$.

We introduce a novel deep representation learning framework grounded in optimal transport (OT) theory, designed to generate robust, low-discrepancy embeddings for high-dimensional data. By leveraging the efficient computation of the Wasserer-2 distance via the Sinkhorn algorithm, our method learns optimal feature representations through a hierarchical, bottom-up strategy. This process begins by establishing pairwise relationships within data clusters, then progressively aggregates these local insights to derive global structure. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines the Betti numbers of random subgraphs within the sparse regime of the complete graph $K_n$. Specifically, we analyze the Erd\`os-R\'enyi random graph $G(n,p)$ and the graph formed by the union of $k$ independent $G(n,p)$ instances, denoted $G_k(n,p)$. Our primary objective is to establish the asymptotic behavior of the normalized Betti numbers for these structures. We demonstrate that, under the condition $p = c/n$ where $c > 1$, the normalized counts for $G(n,p)$ converge in distribution to a Gamma variable. Furthermore, we establish that the normalized counts for $G_k(n,p)$ converge to a Gamma mixture, with the mixing parameters determined by the specific value of $c$.

Robotic systems often rely on visual servoing for object manipulation, yet they frequently lack the capability to precisely estimate their own extrinsic parameters. This paper introduces a learning-based approach to infer the robot's extrinsic parameters directly from a single image. The method employs a convolutional neural network trained on synthetic images generated by simulating a robot grasping objects. Experimental results demonstrate that the trained model can accurately predict extrinsic parameters for real-world images captured by an eye-in-hand camera mounted on a robotic arm.

We introduce Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning (Reverse-RL), a method designed to maximize an objective function subject to a specific constraint. Unlike traditional Constrained Reinforcement Learning (RL), which seeks to maximize a reward while adhering to a cost limit, Reverse-RL flips this dynamic: the agent maximizes a reward function while ensuring a particular metric remains below a defined threshold. This approach is applicable to scenarios where a specific performance metric must be minimized, such as reducing latency or error rates, while simultaneously maximizing another objective like accuracy. We demonstrate that Reverse-RL can be effectively solved using Lagrangian relaxation, which transforms the problem into an unconstrained form. By employing Lagrangian Policy Gradient methods, we can optimize the resulting policy. Furthermore, we present a practical algorithm that iteratively updates both the policy and the Lagrange multiplier to ensure convergence. We validate this method through experiments on a real-world task involving the optimization of a robot's movement, showcasing its efficacy in balancing competing objectives.

The Gaia mission, launched by the European Space Agency in 2013, is designed to create the most comprehensive 3D map of our galaxy to date. By measuring the positions and motions of over a billion stars, it will deliver an unprecedented view of the Milky Way's structure, evolution, and formation history. This paper outlines the mission's objectives, its operational design, and the characteristics of its data products.

The concept of a compact vertex separator, which recursively generates balanced subgraphs to yield treewidth-based algorithms, has been established. This paper introduces a new vertex divider that is balanced around a specific vertex rather than a separator, offering a more straightforward and efficient method for computing vertex-based treewidth measures. Additionally, we present a novel algorithm capable of determining this vertex-based treewidth in $O(n^2)$ time.

This study introduces a generalized framework for modeling weighted directed graphs, designed to accommodate diverse network types characterized by heterogeneous nodes and edges. We establish necessary conditions for these networks to ensure they can be represented as valid weighted directed graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these conditions are sufficient by providing a constructive method to generate such graphs from any set of nodes and edges that meet the criteria.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) across various scientific and engineering disciplines. This study introduces a novel PINN architecture that integrates a posteriori error estimation to ensure the authorization of machine learning predictions. By employing a specialized loss function, the framework estimates the error in the solution of the PDE, thereby enabling the determination of prediction reliability. This mechanism allows the model to designate specific regions as authorized or unauthorized based on data availability, effectively preventing extrapolation into unsupported areas. The proposed approach is validated through two distinct case studies: a linear advection-diffusion equation and a nonlinear Navier-Stokes equation.

This study introduces a machine learning-based atmospheric contamination model designed to analyze transmission dynamics during the COVID-19 pandemic. By leveraging geostatistics and remote sensing data, the model estimates the concentration of airborne SARS-CoV-2 particles within enclosed spaces. The research focuses on the initial phase of outbreaks, specifically the incubation period, to determine how environmental factors influence transmission rates. The findings indicate that atmospheric contamination is a critical driver of COVID-19 spread, with the model successfully predicting the concentration of airborne viral particles in indoor settings. The study also examines the impact of ventilation, air filtration, and other environmental variables on the concentration of airborne SARS-CoV-2 particles. The model was validated using data from a real-world outbreak in a university building in the United States, with the results showing a strong correlation between the predicted and observed concentrations of airborne SARS-CoV-2 particles. The study concludes that the model can be used to predict the transmission of COVID-19 in indoor environments and to identify the environmental factors that influence transmission rates. The study also highlights the importance of ventilation, air filtration, and other environmental variables in reducing the concentration of airborne SARS-CoV-2 particles. This study introduces a novel approach to differentiate Majorana zero-energy peaks from conventional ones, utilizing tunneling spectroscopy with resistive electrodes. The proposed method relies on the observation that, under Ohmic damping conditions, the zero-energy peak in a system with Majorana fermions exhibits a distinct dependence on the resistivity of the electrode compared to other peaks. The analysis employs the Keldysh formalism to derive the differential conductance spectrum for a quantum dot hosting Majorana fermions connected to normal leads. The results indicate that the zero-energy peak's magnitude increases with higher electrode resistivity, whereas conventional peaks diminish. The study further examines the impact of various parameters, including the dot's charging energy, the Majorana coupling strength, and the electrode's work function, on the differential conductance spectrum. The findings suggest that the proposed method offers a straightforward and effective means of distinguishing Majorana zero-energy peaks from other types.

This study investigates linear bandits characterized by varying action sets, where the feasible set is defined as a subset of a larger master polytope. We demonstrate that the standard assumption of a fixed action set is overly restrictive, as the feasible set can change dynamically based on the history of selected actions. To address this, we introduce a new regret metric termed "dynamic regret," which accounts for the evolving nature of the feasible set. We establish that the cumulative regret is bounded by the count of times the feasible set changes multiplied by the maximum regret incurred within any single interval between changes. Furthermore, we show that the standard confidence intervals for the optimal value of the objective function remain valid even when the action set is not predetermined. Consequently, these findings indicate that the uncertainty surrounding the optimal value is unaffected by the adaptivity of the action set.

We demonstrate that in gapped graphene, the orbital Hall effect (OHE) can be observed even when the valley Hall effect (VHE) is absent. This phenomenon arises from the distinct nature of the OHE, which stems from the intrinsic curvature of the Berry connection rather than the non-zero Berry curvature required for VHE. Consequently, the OHE offers a viable alternative to VHE for generating valley-dependent transverse currents in systems lacking Berry curvature.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely utilized for node classification tasks, yet their susceptibility to data poisoning remains a critical vulnerability. This paper investigates the effectiveness of adversaries in corrupting training data to manipulate GNN predictions. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, an adversary can successfully target a specific subset of nodes to force misclassification. Furthermore, we introduce a novel attack strategy that leverages the topological structure of the graph to contaminate data more efficiently. Finally, we propose a defense mechanism designed to mitigate the impact of such poisoning attacks.

We introduce a new method for identifying matches in astronomical catalogs by integrating photometric data from the 2MASS survey with astrometry from Gaia. This approach employs a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to classify color information, which is then used to refine the likelihood of positional matches. The study applies this technique to the Gaia EDR3 catalog, cross-referencing it with 2MASS. The results reveal that 99.99% of the 2MASS sources identified in the Gaia EDR3 catalog are located within 0.1 arcseconds of their original positions. Furthermore, the positional accuracy of these matches improves with brighter magnitudes, with the 2MASS catalog showing superior performance compared to the Gaia EDR3 catalog.

This paper investigates the structure of minimal edge covers in the context of infinite hypergraphs. We demonstrate that every such minimal edge cover in an infinite hypergraph can be expressed as the union of a finite collection of maximal matchings and a finite number of edges. Additionally, we establish the existence of infinite hypergraphs where the ratio between the cardinality of the smallest edge cover and that of the largest matching approaches infinity. Finally, we prove that for any countable graph, the size of the smallest edge cover is exactly equal to the size of the largest matching.

Ontologies serve as a vital mechanism for knowledge representation and semantic interoperability, yet their increasing scale and complexity often hinder human comprehension. While various visualization tools exist to assist users in navigating these large-scale ontologies, they frequently fail to adequately represent non-hierarchical connections. This study introduces OntoPlot, a new visualization framework designed to enhance the understanding of relationships within extensive ontologies. By leveraging a force-directed graph algorithm, OntoPlot dynamically renders ontology structures, offering an interactive environment for exploring both hierarchical and non-hierarchical links. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that OntoPlot achieves superior performance in rendering speed and memory efficiency compared to competing systems.

Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems trained on mismatched data distributions between their training and testing environments often suffer from performance degradation. While semi-supervised learning has emerged as a promising solution to address this domain shift, it typically demands complex architectures and extensive computational resources. This paper introduces a streamlined, end-to-end semi-supervised ASR framework that leverages CycleGAN for effective cross-domain image-to-image translation and cycle consistency. By integrating an inter-domain penalty into the speech recognition model, the proposed method further enhances performance. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves significant improvements over a supervised baseline, delivering a 10.0% relative reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) on the LibriSpeech test-clean dataset.

This paper introduces a new approach to robot navigation that integrates active inference with deep reinforcement learning. We hypothesize that active inference can enhance deep reinforcement learning by providing a principled framework for learning goal-directed behaviors. We demonstrate this by training a mobile robot to navigate a cluttered environment, showing that active inference enables the robot to learn navigation skills with significantly fewer interactions compared to standard deep reinforcement learning methods.

The Soret effect, defined as the generation of a temperature gradient in response to a concentration gradient, is a phenomenon that has been extensively studied in colloidal systems. In these mixtures, the Soret coefficient ($s^T$) is determined by the differential response of solute and solvent to temperature changes. While the Soret effect in hard-sphere colloids is well-understood, it remains poorly characterized in soft colloids, where the Soret coefficient is significantly influenced by the differential mobility of the components. This study focuses on the specific contribution of the differential mobility of the solvent to the Soret coefficient. We demonstrate that the differential mobility of the solvent is governed by the differential response of the solvent's internal degrees of freedom to temperature changes. This insight is validated through molecular dynamics simulations of a model system featuring soft solutes and solvents.

This study introduces a novel approach to automatically evaluating compositional capabilities within neural models by leveraging pre-trained language models (PLMs). We propose a new task called "effective transformer-based composition evaluation," which assesses how well a model can generalize to unseen attribute combinations. This method utilizes PLMs to generate high-quality prompts for a downstream task, such as visual concept generation, and employs a downstream model to produce outputs based on these prompts. We demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10% improvement in performance. Additionally, we provide an in-depth analysis of the impact of various factors, including prompt generation strategies, downstream task selection, and model architecture, on the overall effectiveness of the approach.

Domain adaptation for pedestrian identification (DAPI) has become a significant research focus, with recent advances in metric learning effectively addressing domain shifts. Nevertheless, these methods often suffer from false positives caused by domain-specific background noise, which can severely impact performance. To address this, we introduce Box Re-Ranking (BRR), an unsupervised false positive mitigation strategy. BRR operates by re-ranking feature representations to enhance the discriminability of positive samples while suppressing noise. Specifically, it employs a novel loss function that optimizes the relative ordering of positive pairs against negative pairs. Empirical evaluations on two prominent DAPI datasets demonstrate that BRR achieves substantial performance gains.

This study introduces a novel approach to audio enhancement by integrating deep learning with traditional signal processing. The methodology involves converting audio waveforms into spectrogram images, training a generative adversarial network (GAN) to produce high-fidelity versions of these images, and subsequently reconstructing the audio via time-domain vocoding. The research evaluates the efficacy of this pipeline using both objective and subjective assessments. The findings indicate that the audio quality resulting from this process surpasses that of the original input.

Throwing is a fundamental human action with broad applications, ranging from sports and rehabilitation to robotics and human-robot interaction. While numerous studies have focused on optimizing throwing mechanics to enhance performance, there is limited understanding of how errors in the point of release affect the outcome. This study examines the impact of varying release points on throwing accuracy and consistency, specifically analyzing the relationship between release location and the resulting ball trajectory. We introduce FauxThrow, a simulation framework designed to replicate throwing actions by modeling the release point and imparting appropriate linear and angular velocities to the object. Using this system, we conducted experiments to assess throwing consistency across different release locations. Our findings indicate that the point of release significantly influences throwing consistency, with the optimal location being the tip of the hand. Furthermore, we observed that the ball's spin rate is critical for maintaining trajectory stability.

This study introduces a top-down tree-decoding algorithm for sequence-to-tree models, designed to enhance translation quality by leveraging syntactic links. These links enable the model to capture long-range dependencies during the decoding phase, effectively addressing limitations inherent in standard approaches. We demonstrate that this new algorithm is equivalent to the well-established CKY parsing algorithm, which operates via bottom-up decoding. Furthermore, we show that our method can be integrated into existing sequence-to-tree frameworks with minimal architectural changes. Empirical results confirm that our approach significantly boosts translation performance on the English-French and English-German tasks.

Accurate binding energy data is essential for astrochemical models to simulate the formation of molecules on interstellar dust grains. However, existing databases contain binding energy values that vary significantly, often by orders of magnitude, due to the diverse computational methods and theoretical models employed. To address this uncertainty, we introduce the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a web-based system designed to aggregate binding energy calculations from the literature. BEAP enables users to access binding energy distributions for various molecule-dust grain pairs, thereby facilitating a more robust assessment of uncertainties in astrochemical models.

This study examines a stochastic multiplicative process subject to a non-zero lower bound, analyzing its statistical characteristics and process dynamics. We derive the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) for the process at a specific time $t$, alongside the PDFs for the process's first-passage time relative to this minimum limit. Furthermore, we calculate the mean first-passage time and the probability of the process remaining within defined bounds over a given interval. These theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations.

We introduce a novel quantum algorithm designed to evaluate the expected value of an operator within a quantum state. This algorithm utilizes random Clifford circuits with a shallow depth, offering a significant advantage by requiring only a quadratic increase in gate count relative to the standard quantum phase estimation method. The approach is versatile, capable of estimating the expectation values for any operator, including those that are non-Hermitian. Furthermore, the algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to the quantum simulation of the transverse field Ising model.

This study examines the scattering behavior of the inverse scattering transform applied to the Davey-Stewartson equations, specifically the DS-II variant. We demonstrate that the reflection coefficient exhibits a notable dependence on the magnitude of $k$ for both the reflection and transmission coefficients. This phenomenon arises from the presence of a branch cut in the reflection coefficient within the complex $k$-plane, which originates from the continuous spectrum of the associated linear operator. Our findings offer valuable insights into the scattering properties of the inverse scattering transform for these equations, with potential applications in diverse fields such as fluid dynamics and plasma physics.

This study introduces Sibylvariant, a new text classification framework that leverages Sibyl graphs to represent document structures. By utilizing a graph-based approach, the framework captures the inherent relationships within documents. We further propose Sibylvariant, which offers two distinct modifications to enhance the robustness of graph-based classifiers. The first modification involves a graph-based feature selection technique designed to identify the most informative nodes for classification. The second modification utilizes a graph-based ensemble method to aggregate predictions from multiple subgraphs. Empirical results demonstrate that Sibylvariant significantly outperforms the original Sibyl framework, achieving superior accuracy in text classification tasks.

This study introduces a novel meta-learning framework for linear illustrations, where the objective is to train a generator capable of producing linear drawings for unseen objects. The method relies on a robust loss function that enforces linearity and incorporates a novel regularization term to ensure smoothness across the latent space. The resulting model achieves state-of-the-art performance on both quantitative and qualitative assessments. Furthermore, the authors showcase the method's versatility by applying it to tasks such as generating linear sketches of animals from text descriptions and creating linear patterns for 3D models based on point clouds.

Neural machine translation (NMT) models are typically trained with substantial computational resources, yet their deployment often relies on lighter-weight architectures. This paper investigates the stability of NMT models during the extraction and quantization processes, which are essential for creating lightweight, low-resource translation systems. We conducted a comprehensive study on quantization and model extraction across various architectures, including Transformer, RNN, and CNN models, as well as different bit-widths and extraction techniques. Our findings indicate that while quantization is generally more stable than model extraction, the latter yields significantly smaller model sizes. Consequently, we recommend a hybrid strategy that combines both methods to achieve the most compact and efficient NMT models.

Deep learning methods have proven highly effective for medical image segmentation, yet their application in clinical settings is often hindered by the substantial labeled data required for training. This study investigates whether image enhancement techniques can reduce that dependency. We evaluate three specific approaches: (1) training on augmented images, (2) training on denoised images, and (3) training on both augmented and denoised images. Experiments were conducted on the NIH Chest X-ray dataset using pneumonia segmentation as the target task. Results indicate that employing augmentation and denoising strategies significantly lowers the necessity for labeled data compared to standard training.

Prompt tuning has recently emerged as a highly effective approach for adapting pre-trained language models (PLMs) to specific downstream tasks. This study investigates its application in image description generation, demonstrating that prompt tuning can regulate the diversity and coherence of the resulting descriptions. We introduce a novel method, REGID (Regulatable Image Description via Prompt Tuning), which leverages this capability to generate descriptions with adjustable levels of diversity and coherence. Additionally, we present a new dataset, Diverse Image Descriptions (DIVAD), featuring varied descriptions for the same images to facilitate the evaluation of descriptive diversity. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks while offering a flexible mechanism to control output characteristics.

This paper offers a novel perspective on the concept of "damage" within the realm of causal inference. We introduce a new definition of damage that is more general than the traditional definition, which relies on the assumption of a specific threshold. We demonstrate that the traditional definition is merely a particular instance of our proposed framework. We also establish a link between our definition and the established literature on treatment effects for heterogeneous populations. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our approach by applying it to the analysis of the effects of the 2008 financial crisis.

This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new deep learning framework built on Microsoft Spark MLlib. It offers a comprehensive suite of tools for designing, training, and deploying deep learning models across diverse architectures, including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). MMLSpark is designed to be highly adaptable and scalable, supporting various neural network topologies and activation functions, and capable of handling both tabular and image data. It also features an expandable architecture that allows users to easily add new layers and custom components. The framework's flexibility enables the creation of complex models with multiple hidden layers, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. The paper provides a detailed overview of MMLSpark's capabilities and demonstrates its effectiveness through several case studies. The paper concludes with a discussion of the framework's limitations and potential areas for future research. Voice conversion (VC) and speech translation (ST) are distinct tasks that, individually, require extensive datasets and annotated resources. This paper introduces a unified framework capable of performing both functions simultaneously in a zero-shot manner, eliminating the need for task-specific training data. By leveraging a pre-trained large-scale multilingual speech model, our approach synthesizes speech in unseen target languages and styles without prior exposure to those targets. We evaluate our method against state-of-the-art techniques on both zero-shot and few-shot benchmarks, demonstrating that our system achieves superior performance.

This study examines a Coleman-Gurtin type model featuring dynamic boundary constraints, where heat exchange between a body and its environment is governed by Newton's law of cooling. The model incorporates a dynamic boundary condition that links the boundary heat flux to the rate of change in a thermal variable, reflecting the energy balance between the material and its surroundings. The existence and uniqueness of solutions are established using semigroup theory and variational methods. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the asymptotic behavior of the system as time tends to infinity, demonstrating that the solution converges to a steady state under appropriate assumptions.

Accurate load forecasting is essential for the efficient operation of distribution networks, particularly as the integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) increases. This study introduces a novel forecasting approach for low-voltage networks that utilizes a fusion of daily peak forecasts and probabilistic short-term predictions. The proposed method is evaluated against actual data from a real distribution transformer, demonstrating that the combined strategy outperforms standalone daily peak forecasts and significantly surpasses the accuracy of short-term probabilistic models alone.

This paper outlines a blueprint for synthesizing machine learning (ML) and domain expertise to create robust, reliable, and interpretable models. We introduce a structured framework that guides domain experts through the entire ML lifecycle, from problem definition to model deployment. This approach enables experts to effectively contribute to every stage, resulting in models that are both performant and aligned with domain-specific needs.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant global loss of life, with chest CT scans serving as a critical diagnostic tool for identifying the disease. However, the scarcity of high-quality, annotated CT datasets hinders the development of effective lesion localization and segmentation models. This study introduces a weakly supervised approach to address this challenge by leveraging only image-level labels. By utilizing a novel loss function, the model learns to localize lesions without requiring pixel-level annotations. Experimental results demonstrate that this method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised techniques. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness against data distribution shifts, maintaining consistent performance across different datasets.

Automated spine analysis is essential for clinical workflows, yet current methods often struggle with intervertebral disc issues, scoliosis, and vertebral fractures. This study introduces a novel vertebral localization and recognition framework that rectifies the spine and employs anatomically constrained optimization. The proposed method utilizes a spine rectification module to align the spine with a predefined 3D template, followed by a vertebral recognition module that identifies vertebrae by optimizing a cost function based on anatomical constraints. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in both localization and recognition tasks.

We investigate the nonlinear interaction between a single electron and a cavity field, specifically examining the electron's scattering dynamics within the ultrastrong coupling regime. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to standard expectations, the electron's motion can be dynamically stabilized by the cavity field. This stabilization arises from the electron's quantum oscillations, which are driven by the nonlinear interaction and can be observed in the electron's trajectory. Our findings demonstrate that the electron's motion can be controlled by adjusting the cavity field parameters, such as the field's amplitude and phase. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the nonlinear interaction between electrons and cavity fields, which is crucial for the development of quantum technologies.

This study introduces a reinforcement learning method for controlling elastic actuators in legged robots, specifically focusing on a quadruped with series elastic actuators (SEAs). The primary objective is to enhance locomotion stability and energy efficiency by automatically tuning actuator parameters, such as stiffness and damping, during the swing phase. The proposed approach employs a neural network to estimate optimal SEA configurations based on the robot's current state, with training conducted using a physics-based simulator. Experimental results demonstrate that the learned control policy effectively leverages these elastic actuators to achieve stable and energy-efficient walking.

This study examines the problem of distinguishing between two non-orthogonal quantum states, $\rho$ and $\sigma$, by analyzing the upper bound of their optimal distinguishability. We introduce a variational approach to derive this limit, which involves optimizing over a specific class of positive operator-valued measures (POVMs). The method yields an upper bound expressed as the solution to a semidefinite program (SDP). Furthermore, we demonstrate that this SDP formulation is mathematically equivalent to the Jamiolkowski-Iommi-Wootters (JW) inequality, which provides the tightest known upper bound for distinguishing two quantum states.

This study examines the fundamental physics of a proposed small-scale tearing instability in collisionless plasmas, which operates within a slab geometry featuring a current sheet and a constant magnetic shear. The analysis reveals that the tearing mode is driven by a free energy source arising from the anisotropy of the parallel temperature ($T_{\parallel}$) across the current sheet. The resulting growth rate is proportional to the magnitude of this $T_{\parallel}$ temperature gradient. Furthermore, the paper investigates the impact of electron heat conduction on the mode's evolution, demonstrating that the tearing mode remains stable when the electron thermal conductivity is sufficiently high.

Fashion image retrieval (FIR) is a critical task within the fashion industry, yet existing methods often struggle with the scarcity of labeled data and the high cost of annotation. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised feature-level trait manipulation (SFM) framework designed to enhance retrieval performance. Our approach leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) to modify image embeddings within a latent space, enabling the synthesis of diverse visual traits such as color, texture, and style. By training a retrieval model on these augmented embeddings, the system learns robust representations that generalize well to unseen trait variations. Experimental results demonstrate that SFM significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques across multiple datasets. Furthermore, the method exhibits strong robustness against noisy labels, underscoring its potential for practical deployment in real-world scenarios.

This study introduces a novel dual gradient descent method designed to address linear ill-posed problems within the framework of Banach spaces. We establish the convergence of this approach for a broad spectrum of data fidelity metrics, including the $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_\infty$ norms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed dual gradient scheme is mathematically equivalent to the primal proximal gradient method, thereby confirming its convergence to the optimal solution.

This paper introduces a novel synthetic dataset designed to train light field depth estimation models, featuring complex real-world occlusions and depth discontinuities. To generate this data, we developed a new 3D asset creation tool that supports occlusion-aware expense modeling. By utilizing a Monte Carlo renderer, the system produces high-quality synthetic light field data. Experimental results demonstrate that models trained on this dataset achieve superior performance compared to those trained on existing datasets.
We establish the bilinear method for the Fokas-Lenells formula by deriving the relevant Fay's identity.

We derive non-Riemannian gravitational actions by applying the double field theory (DFT) formalism to the Dyer-Khuri-Roiban (DKR) double field theory framework. This process yields a class of non-Riemannian geometries that encompasses the non-Riemannian geometries identified in the non-Riemannian Hořava-Lifshitz gravity (NLHG) model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the NLHG action can be obtained from this gravitational action by imposing the NLHG ansatz.

This study introduces a novel method for dynamically selecting Access Points (APs) or wireless extenders in residential environments by leveraging Channel Load (CL) metrics. The proposed approach utilizes IEEE 802.11k/v protocols to gather real-time CL data from neighboring APs, enabling clients to choose the optimal connection. The research evaluates the performance of this mechanism through both simulations and experimental trials. The findings indicate that the proposed scheme outperforms conventional selection methods, delivering superior throughput and lower latency.
